title: Removal of Regulations Limiting Authorizations To Proceed With Construction Activities Pending Rehearing
summary:
Two federal agencies issued notable final rules: one to address a safety issue on hot air balloons, and another to speed up approvals for natural gas projects while keeping case-by-case protections in place.

On aviation safety, the Federal Aviation Administration is requiring operators of hot air balloons to check a specific fuel cylinder valve adaptor for cracks before every flight and replace it with a newer part at the next scheduled inspection or immediately if a crack is found. This aims to prevent gas leaks that could lead to fire and emergency landings. The rule takes effect October 27, 2025, and applies across many balloon brands. Owners or pilots can do the visual checks and must log them, and special flight permits aren’t allowed if a problem is found. Who benefits: balloon passengers, pilots, and the public, thanks to reduced fire risk. Who may be negatively affected: balloon owners and operators who face added preflight checks, potential grounding if damage is found, and the cost and downtime to swap the part.

On energy infrastructure, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission removed a rule that had automatically blocked construction authorizations for natural gas pipelines and liquefied natural gas facilities while requests for reconsideration were pending. The agency says this change will cut months of delay, help projects deliver capacity when it’s needed, and support grid reliability as electricity and gas demand grow. It also points to a court decision that allows opponents to quickly seek judicial review and emergency stays, and it will continue to consider stays and extra safeguards on a case-by-case basis—especially where landowners could face eminent domain and ask for a pause. The change takes effect November 10, 2025. Who benefits: project developers, contractors, and energy customers who could see faster timelines, potentially lower costs, and improved reliability. Who may be negatively affected: landowners, local communities, and environmental groups who worry construction could begin before all challenges are resolved, raising concerns about property impacts, environmental harm, and public trust. They still can seek Commission stays and court orders, but some view the prior, across-the-board pause as a clearer protection.

In short, one rule tightens safety for balloon flights; the other trims procedural delays for gas projects while leaving targeted protections in place.
